doc.title: Howie Shear interviewed by Monk Rowe, Dunkirk, New York, October 11, 2014

title: Advice to students: be prepared and diversify
summary: Shear stresses preparedness with CDs and date books, brokering lessons and contracting so he never needed a day job.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Advice to young musicians starting out

blocks.x: Absolutely. When I give clinics I always speak about that. It’s very important. It’s as important as playing well.
So what do you tell a student not to do?

Don’t be unprepared. Be prepared. Now I have several bags/satchels in my car at home in Los Angeles. And I have everything I’ve ever written on CDs. I’ve written everything from children’s books with music, to hard bop jazz quartet albums, to film scoring, jingles, and things like that. And if I run into somebody, which you always do in Los Angeles, especially in the town I live in. I have stuff to give them right away. Because if you say oh are you going to be around tomorrow — you’ll never see them again. And if you’re not prepared with stuff — and it’s so easy to be prepared now, you just burn CDs on your home laptop. You don’t have to go into these places and pay big money. It’s practically free. So I’m always burning CDs, I see what I’m lacking and oh I need more of those or more of those. And I’m constantly preparing. Yeah. You want that? You want that? You want that? Here it is. And that way they know that they don’t have to go shopping for it and calling 50 people up, “you got something like this, I mean, for a scene in a movie?” It’s right away. And so you have to be prepared. Yeah. You have to have date books. I know you have electronic phones now and cell phones and pads and all this stuff, but you still need, I think, cards, business cards, or something. Because a lot of times people will lose information on electric devices, you know IPads or the cloud will eat it up or something, and who knows. So I still have paper stuff I give people. I have a date book, I write in a date book. I don’t use my phone for those things. I use my phone for a phone.
It’s probably our generation I suppose, they don’t want to let go of that.

You know I’ve got a lot of students that are in college. I teach at several universities and I teach privately. And they’re constantly forgetting things. I still don’t forget anything. And yet they have all the devices and they know how to use them as well as anybody, and they are still forgetting things. And they set alarms and reminders and I don’t understand that but, you know, so, it might be a generation thing but they’re still forgetting a lot more than I forget. And I write it down with a pencil in my date book. But you’ve just got to be prepared with everything that you need for the business of music. And I also have a motto, “don’t turn anything down.” If someone comes up to me, which has happened, a parent and says my child is playing cello, could you teach cello. Well I can’t teach cello but I say yes, sure. And what I do is I find her or the parent a cello teacher for their child. I’m brokering the deal. As long as the cello teacher shows up that’s all you need. And that way you could start another business, which I have, by contracting. So I give the cello teacher $50 and I’ll make $25 — not of the $50, I’ll charge $75 for the lesson, and I could make some money with the legwork that I do contracting musicians. So I not only can give musicians work but I also make a little money and that’s how music offices have started. If someone wants a band for their wedding, yeah I could do that. I’ve done that thousands of times. I know the best players
in town and have a band for their wedding. Whatever you need to do so you can stay in the game and you don’t have to get a day job it’s called. And I’ve never had to do anything else.
I just was going to ask that.
No I never had to do anything else after I moved to Los Angeles.
